FARRA:v3p259#2/r10.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v3p259#2/r10.speaker: بعضهم
FARRA:v3p259#2/r10.claim: An unnamed poet's line uses a verb without its final yāʾ, attesting the deletion pattern.

FARRA:v3p259#2/r11.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v3p259#2/r11.speaker: آخر
FARRA:v3p259#2/r11.claim: A second poet similarly omits final yāʾ in a verse about generosity and miserliness.

FARRA:v3p259#2/r7.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v3p259#2/r7.speaker: author
FARRA:v3p259#2/r7.claim: The night in “when it travels” is the night of Muzdalifa.

FARRA:v3p259#2/r8.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v3p259#2/r8.speaker: القراء
FARRA:v3p259#2/r8.claim: Readers vary between retaining the yāʾ in yasrī and dropping it in yasr.

FARRA:v3p259#2/r9.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v3p259#2/r9.speaker: author
FARRA:v3p259#2/r9.claim: He prefers dropping yāʾ because it matches the verse endings and Arabic often keeps only the preceding kasra when deleting yāʾ.

MAJAZ:v2p297/r3.author: Abū ʿUbayda Maʿmar b. al-Muthannā
MAJAZ:v2p297/r3.speaker: author
MAJAZ:v2p297/r3.claim: Yasri drops its yāʾ in the nominative; la adr is a parallel example.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p370/r1.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p370/r1.speaker: قتادة
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p370/r1.claim: Qatada glosses the night as it moves or passes.

ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p370/r2.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Ṣanʿānī
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p370/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
ABDURRAZZAQ:v3p370/r2.claim: Ibn Abbas advises fasting the ninth and tenth days to differ from the Jews.

TUSTARI:89:4/r1.author: Sahl al-Tustarī
TUSTARI:89:4/r1.speaker: author
TUSTARI:89:4/r1.claim: The passing night of the gathering takes away what it contains.

TUSTARI:89:4/r3.author: Sahl al-Tustarī
TUSTARI:89:4/r3.speaker: author
TUSTARI:89:4/r3.claim: Inwardly, the night is Muhammad’s community, the vast multitude.

TUSTARI:89:4/r4.author: Sahl al-Tustarī
TUSTARI:89:4/r4.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
TUSTARI:89:4/r4.claim: A report says that during the Night Journey the Prophet saw a vast multitude between heaven and earth; Gabriel identified them as his community, including seventy thousand who enter Paradise without reckoning, untouched by sins or worldly defilement and knowing only God.

TAB-FULL:v24p358/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p358/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v24p358/r1.claim: The night is described as it travels away and passes; this is the usual Arabic sense of the verb.

TAB-FULL:v24p358/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p358/r2.speaker: عبد الله بن الزبير، ابن عباس، مجاهد، أبو العالية، قتادة، ابن زيد
TAB-FULL:v24p358/r2.claim: These interpreters gloss the night as moving, going, or passing away.

TAB-FULL:v24p358/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p358/r3.speaker: عكرمة
TAB-FULL:v24p358/r3.claim: A distinct interpretation identifies the night with the night at Muzdalifah.

TAB-FULL:v24p358/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p358/r4.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v24p358/r4.claim: He prefers omitting the final yāʾ because it matches the rhyme of the verse endings; Arabic can drop this yāʾ in a raised form when the preceding kasra indicates it.

TAB-FULL:v24p358/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v24p358/r5.speaker: شاعر غير مسمى
TAB-FULL:v24p358/r5.claim: A line of poetry illustrates the Arabic omission of the yāʾ in a raised verb form.

IBNABIHATIM:v10p3425/r1.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3425/r1.speaker: عبد الله بن الزبير
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3425/r1.claim: Ibn al-Zubayr glosses the night as it travels.

IBNABIHATIM:v10p3425/r2.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3425/r2.speaker: مجاهد
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3425/r2.claim: Mujahid likewise glosses the night as it travels.

IBNABIHATIM:v10p3425/r3.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3425/r3.speaker: محمد بن كعب القرظي
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3425/r3.claim: Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi recites the phrase as a command to travel by night, saying its path becomes visible only at Jamʿ.

IBNABIHATIM:v10p3425/r4.author: Ibn Abī Ḥātim al-Rāzī
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3425/r4.speaker: عكرمة
IBNABIHATIM:v10p3425/r4.claim: Ikrimah identifies the night as the night of Jamʿ.

NAHHAS:v5p219/r1.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p219/r1.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v5p219/r1.claim: The original form is yasrī; its yāʾ is omitted in writing as a verse ending, while connected recitation may restore it and pausing follows the muṣḥaf spelling.

NAHHAS:v5p219/r2.author: Abū Jaʿfar al-Naḥḥās
NAHHAS:v5p219/r2.speaker: author
NAHHAS:v5p219/r2.claim: A good interpretation is that the night approaches as the day withdraws.

FARISI-HUJJA:v6p403/r1.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p403/r1.speaker: ابن كثير
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p403/r1.claim: Ibn Kathīr retains yāʾ in both connection and pause in يسر and جابوا الصخر.

FARISI-HUJJA:v6p403/r2.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p403/r2.speaker: نافع
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p403/r2.claim: Nāfiʿ retains yāʾ in connection but drops it at a pause.

FARISI-HUJJA:v6p403/r3.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p403/r3.speaker: ابن عامر وعاصم وحمزة والكسائي
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p403/r3.claim: These four readers omit yāʾ in both connection and pause; Abū ʿUbaydah says al-Kisāʾī formerly retained it before returning to omission.

FARISI-HUJJA:v6p403/r4.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p403/r4.speaker: أبو عمرو
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p403/r4.claim: Reports differ about Abū ʿAmr: one says he omits yāʾ in both positions, another says he retains it only when connecting, and another says he adds it within an āyah but pauses without it at the verse end.

FARISI-HUJJA:v6p403/r5.author: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p403/r5.speaker: اليزيدي
FARISI-HUJJA:v6p403/r5.claim: Al-Yazīdī says connection has yāʾ and silent pause omits it, following the written form.

THALABI:v10p194/r10.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p194/r10.speaker: ابن عامر وعاصم وأبو عبيد
THALABI:v10p194/r10.claim: They omit the final yāʾ in both connected and paused recitation, with Abu Ubayd choosing this form to follow the written rasm.

THALABI:v10p194/r11.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p194/r11.speaker: ابن كثير ويعقوب
THALABI:v10p194/r11.claim: They retain the yāʾ in both connected and paused recitation, following the original form.

THALABI:v10p194/r12.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p194/r12.speaker: الخليل بن أحمد
THALABI:v10p194/r12.claim: He says the yāʾ is omitted to match the verse endings.

THALABI:v10p194/r13.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p194/r13.speaker: أكثر أهل المعاني
THALABI:v10p194/r13.claim: They construe the night as something people travel through, like a night described as sleeping; the phrase omits the yāʾ as Arabic may do.

THALABI:v10p194/r14.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p194/r14.speaker: الفراء
THALABI:v10p194/r14.claim: He says Arabs delete the yāʾ and rely on the kasra before it, citing poetry.

THALABI:v10p194/r6.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p194/r6.speaker: أكثر المفسرين
THALABI:v10p194/r6.claim: They interpret the night as moving away and departing.

THALABI:v10p194/r7.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p194/r7.speaker: قتادة
THALABI:v10p194/r7.claim: He interprets the night as arriving and coming on.

THALABI:v10p194/r8.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p194/r8.speaker: مجاهد وعكرمة والكلبي
THALABI:v10p194/r8.claim: They identify the night as the night at Muzdalifa.

THALABI:v10p194/r9.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p194/r9.speaker: أهل المدينة وأبو عمرو وعيسى
THALABI:v10p194/r9.claim: They pronounce the final yāʾ in yسر during connected recitation; Abu Hatim chooses this, while Abu Ubayd reports al-Kisai later dropped it in both positions to match the verse ending.

THALABI:v10p195/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p195/r3.speaker: الأخفش
THALABI:v10p195/r3.claim: He explains that the night itself does not travel; rather, travel happens in it, and its grammatical form loses inflection, like بغيا for باغية.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p265/r18.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p265/r18.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p265/r18.claim: The night may be the Night of Decree because mercy travels through it and it has increased reward.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p265/r19.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p265/r19.speaker: محمد بن كعب
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p265/r19.claim: It may be the night of Muzdalifa, when people gather to obey God; Muhammad ibn Kab explains that travelers should spend the night at Jam, meaning Muzdalifa.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p265/r20.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p265/r20.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p265/r20.claim: It may refer to the night generally.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p265/r21.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p265/r21.speaker: ابن عباس
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p265/r21.claim: يَسْر means that the night becomes dark.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p265/r22.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p265/r22.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p265/r22.claim: It may mean that the night travels with the sun and heavens from one horizon to another.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p265/r23.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p265/r23.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p265/r23.claim: It may mean that people travel during the night, since السرى is night travel.

QUSHAYRI:v3p419/r9.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v3p419/r9.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v3p419/r9.claim: The night that moves on simply passes away.

WAHIDI-QT:89:4/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-QT:89:4/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-QT:89:4/r1.claim: The night is the night of Muzdalifa when it has passed and gone.

WAHIDI-QT:89:4/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-QT:89:4/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-QT:89:4/r2.claim: An alternative takes the phrase as the night when it comes and approaches.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:89:1-6/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:89:1-6/r4.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:89:1-6/r4.claim: The passing night is the night at Muzdalifa as it leaves; another view says when it arrives.

JISHUMI:v10p7395/r10.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v10p7395/r10.speaker: الأخفش
JISHUMI:v10p7395/r10.claim: He says deleting the yāʾ is irregular because the word is a verb; deletion is expected in nouns, not verbs.

JISHUMI:v10p7395/r11.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v10p7395/r11.speaker: الخليل
JISHUMI:v10p7395/r11.claim: He explains deletion of the yāʾ as matching the verse endings.

JISHUMI:v10p7395/r12.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v10p7395/r12.speaker: المؤرج
JISHUMI:v10p7395/r12.claim: He reports al-Akhfash's explanation that night is not itself the traveler; it is the time in which people travel.

JISHUMI:v10p7395/r6.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v10p7395/r6.speaker: أبو جعفر ونافع وأبو عمرو وقتيبة عن الكسائي
JISHUMI:v10p7395/r6.claim: They retain the yāʾ in yasrī when linking, but omit it when stopping.

JISHUMI:v10p7395/r7.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v10p7395/r7.speaker: ابن كثير ويعقوب
JISHUMI:v10p7395/r7.claim: They retain the yāʾ in yasrī both when linking and when stopping.

JISHUMI:v10p7395/r8.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v10p7395/r8.speaker: عاصم وابن عامر والكسائي وحمزة
JISHUMI:v10p7395/r8.claim: They omit the yāʾ in both connected and paused reading; Abū ʿUbayd reports that al-Kisāʾī later settled on this omission.

JISHUMI:v10p7395/r9.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v10p7395/r9.speaker: أبو حاتم
JISHUMI:v10p7395/r9.claim: He prefers retaining the yāʾ when linking and omitting it at pause, while omission is also explained by the written form, ease, and rhyme.

BAGHAWI:89:4/r1.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI:89:4/r1.speaker: author
BAGHAWI:89:4/r1.claim: The night as it yasri means as it moves away or departs, as in the verse about the night when it departs.

BAGHAWI:89:4/r2.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI:89:4/r2.speaker: قتادة
BAGHAWI:89:4/r2.claim: Qatada says it means when night arrives and comes on; the intended sense is every night.

BAGHAWI:89:4/r3.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI:89:4/r3.speaker: مجاهد وعكرمة والكلبي
BAGHAWI:89:4/r3.claim: Mujahid, Ikrima, and al-Kalbi identify it as the night of Muzdalifa.

BAGHAWI:89:4/r4.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI:89:4/r4.speaker: قراء أهل الحجاز والبصرة
BAGHAWI:89:4/r4.claim: Readers in the Hijaz and Basra pronounce the final ya in yasri when continuing; Ibn Kathir and Ya'qub also retain it when pausing, while the rest omit it in both positions.

BAGHAWI:89:4/r5.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI:89:4/r5.speaker: author
BAGHAWI:89:4/r5.claim: The ya is omitted to preserve the rhyme endings, but retained by others because it is the root letter and verbs do not normally lose it at a pause.

BAGHAWI:89:4/r6.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI:89:4/r6.speaker: الأخفش
BAGHAWI:89:4/r6.claim: Al-Akhfash explains the missing ya by saying the night does not itself travel; people travel in it, so the verb is treated as diverted from its ordinary sense.

BAGHAWI:89:4/r7.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI:89:4/r7.speaker: الأخفش
BAGHAWI:89:4/r7.claim: Al-Akhfash compares the inflectional reduction to Maryam 19:28, where baghiy is used instead of baghiyya because the word is treated as shortened from baghiya.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p417/r1.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p417/r1.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p417/r1.claim: The night goes and departs, as in the verse about night’s departure; Qatada instead says it arrives, and either way the reference is every night.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p417/r2.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p417/r2.speaker: قتادة
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p417/r2.claim: Qatada says the night arrives and comes forward.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p417/r3.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p417/r3.speaker: مجاهد وعكرمة والكلبي
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p417/r3.claim: They interpret the night as the night of Muzdalifa.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p417/r4.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p417/r4.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p417/r4.claim: Hijaz and Basra readers pronounce the final ya in connection; Ibn Kathir and Yaqub retain it at pause too, while others delete it in both positions.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p417/r5.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p417/r5.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p417/r5.claim: Deleting the ya suits verse-end rhyme; retaining it preserves the verb’s root letter, normally kept at pause, as in ‘he judges.’

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p417/r6.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p417/r6.speaker: الأخفش
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p417/r6.claim: Al-Akhfash says the ya drops because night does not travel itself but is traveled through; he compares بغيا without final ta to بغية.

KASHSHAF:89:4/r1.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:89:4/r1.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:89:4/r1.claim: After swearing by specified nights, God swears by night generally as it passes, as in two other night oaths.

KASHSHAF:89:4/r5.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:89:4/r5.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:89:4/r5.claim: The tanwin on yasri substitutes for the extended alif of poetic-style vowel lengthening.

KASHSHAF:89:4/r7.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:89:4/r7.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:89:4/r7.claim: The yāʾ in yasri drops in connected speech because the kasra suffices, and at pause both the yāʾ and kasra drop.

KASHSHAF:89:4/r8.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:89:4/r8.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:89:4/r8.claim: Another interpretation supplies a preposition: the night travels within it.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p749/r6.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p749/r6.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p749/r6.claim: The general night is sworn by when it passes, as in other descriptions of the departing night.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p749/r8.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p749/r8.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p749/r8.claim: Another reading joins al-fajr and al-watr with tanwin, which substitutes for a final lengthening letter; Ibn Abbas reads ليال عشر with an annexation meaning nights of ten days.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p749/r9.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p749/r9.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p749/r9.claim: The yāʾ in يسر is dropped in connected speech because the kasra suffices, and in pause it is omitted with the kasra; another interpretation means ‘moves along in it.’

TABRISI:89:1-30#4/r10.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:89:1-30#4/r10.speaker: author
TABRISI:89:1-30#4/r10.claim: Another explanation says the night moves with the sun as it travels between horizons.

TABRISI:89:1-30#4/r11.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:89:1-30#4/r11.speaker: قتادة والجبائي
TABRISI:89:1-30#4/r11.claim: They interpret “when it moves” as each night arriving and coming toward us.

TABRISI:89:1-30#4/r12.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:89:1-30#4/r12.speaker: مجاهد وعكرمة والكلبي
TABRISI:89:1-30#4/r12.claim: A particular night is identified as the night of Muzdalifa: pilgrims travel from Arafah, pray there at dawn, and leave for Mina.

TABRISI:89:1-30#4/r9.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:89:1-30#4/r9.speaker: author
TABRISI:89:1-30#4/r9.claim: The night may mean every night departing as darkness gives way to light; its ordered course and arrival of light point to God's majesty.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p108/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p108/r1.speaker: ابن كثير ويعقوب
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p108/r1.claim: They read yasrī with yāʾ both when pausing and continuing; Nāfiʿ and Abū ʿAmr agree when continuing.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p108/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p108/r2.speaker: ابن عامر وعاصم وحمزة والكسائي
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p108/r2.claim: They read yasr without yāʾ both when pausing and continuing.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p108/r3.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p108/r3.speaker: الفراء والزجاج
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p108/r3.claim: They prefer omitting yāʾ, to match the verse endings and the written muṣḥaf.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p108/r4.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p108/r4.speaker: الجمهور، الزجاج
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p108/r4.claim: Taking night as the subject, the preferred meaning is that night goes away.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p108/r5.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p108/r5.speaker: قتادة
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p108/r5.claim: Taking night as the subject, another reading is that night comes on.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p108/r6.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p108/r6.speaker: الأخفش وابن قتيبة
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p108/r6.claim: Alternatively, the verb's subject is something moving through the night, as in calling a night nāʾim when people sleep in it.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p108/r7.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p108/r7.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p108/r7.claim: The oath most naturally refers to every night.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p108/r8.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p108/r8.speaker: مجاهد وعكرمة
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p108/r8.claim: It may refer specifically to the night of Muzdalifa, the Night of Gathering.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p108/r9.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p108/r9.speaker: الماوردي
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p108/r9.claim: Another interpretation is the Night of Decree.

RAZI:89:4/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:89:4/r1.speaker: author
RAZI:89:4/r1.claim: Here يسري means that the night moves on, passes, and comes to its end.

RAZI:89:4/r10.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:89:4/r10.speaker: الزجاج
RAZI:89:4/r10.claim: Al-Zajjaj reports a reading that retains the final yāʾ in يسري, but prefers its deletion because verse endings commonly drop yāʾs and the kasra signals it.

RAZI:89:4/r11.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:89:4/r11.speaker: الفراء
RAZI:89:4/r11.claim: Al-Farraʾ says Arabs may delete yāʾ and rely on the preceding kasra; he adduces poetic usage as evidence.

RAZI:89:4/r12.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:89:4/r12.speaker: author
RAZI:89:4/r12.claim: The cited poem’s form تعط exemplifies yāʾ deletion, which is especially apt at a verse ending.

RAZI:89:4/r13.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:89:4/r13.speaker: أبو علي
RAZI:89:4/r13.claim: Abu Ali explains that pauses and rhyme endings permit change: even sound consonants change at pauses, so letters resembling additions may also be deleted.

RAZI:89:4/r14.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:89:4/r14.speaker: من أثبت الياء
RAZI:89:4/r14.claim: Those retaining yāʾ in both connected and paused speech argue that verbs keep it at pause, unlike nouns such as قاض and غاز.

RAZI:89:4/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:89:4/r2.speaker: author
RAZI:89:4/r2.claim: Another lexical explanation takes the night’s going as traveling through it.

RAZI:89:4/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:89:4/r3.speaker: قتادة
RAZI:89:4/r3.claim: Qatada interprets يسري as the night arriving and drawing near.

RAZI:89:4/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:89:4/r4.speaker: أكثر المفسرين
RAZI:89:4/r4.claim: Most exegetes understand the oath as referring to night generally, not one particular night, comparing other general descriptions of night.

RAZI:89:4/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:89:4/r5.speaker: author
RAZI:89:4/r5.claim: The alternation of night and day and their changing lengths are a great blessing and signs of a wise, all-knowing director, making night worthy of an oath.

RAZI:89:4/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:89:4/r6.speaker: مقاتل
RAZI:89:4/r6.claim: Mقاتل identifies the night as the night of Muzdalifa and reads يسري as travel taking place within it, like a night named for sleeping or staying awake in it.

RAZI:89:4/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:89:4/r7.speaker: author
RAZI:89:4/r7.claim: The journey through that night begins with departure from Arafat for Muzdalifa.

RAZI:89:4/r8.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:89:4/r8.speaker: النبي
RAZI:89:4/r8.claim: A report says the Prophet brought forward his vulnerable family members during this night.

RAZI:89:4/r9.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:89:4/r9.speaker: الشافعي
RAZI:89:4/r9.claim: Al-Shafi‘i allows this early departure only after the middle of the night.

RAZI-FULL:v31p149#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v31p149#2/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v31p149#2/r1.claim: Yasri can mean the night passes, like 74:33 and 81:17, or can mean traveling through the night; Qatada takes it as night arriving.

RAZI-FULL:v31p149#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v31p149#2/r2.speaker: أكثر المفسرين
RAZI-FULL:v31p149#2/r2.claim: Most exegetes take the verse as the night in general: alternating night and day is a great divine benefit and evidence of a wise, knowing governor.

RAZI-FULL:v31p149#2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v31p149#2/r3.speaker: مقاتل
RAZI-FULL:v31p149#2/r3.claim: Muqatil identifies the night as the night at Muzdalifa, when pilgrims travel; the Prophet sent weaker family members ahead, and Shafiʿi permits this after midnight.

RAZI-FULL:v31p149#2/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v31p149#2/r4.speaker: الزجاج
RAZI-FULL:v31p149#2/r4.claim: Al-Zajjaj says a reading retains the final ya; he prefers deleting it at a verse ending because pauses commonly omit final ya.

RAZI-FULL:v31p149#2/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v31p149#2/r5.speaker: الفراء
RAZI-FULL:v31p149#2/r5.claim: Al-Farra says Arabic may drop ya and rely on the preceding kasra, citing a poetic example.

RAZI-FULL:v31p149#2/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v31p149#2/r6.speaker: أبو علي
RAZI-FULL:v31p149#2/r6.claim: Abu Ali explains omission at pauses and rhyme: pauses alter sounds, so letters resembling additions can be deleted; readers retaining ya argue that final ya remains in verbs.

QURTUBI-FULL:89:4-5#2/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:89:4-5#2/r1.speaker: الزمخشري
QURTUBI-FULL:89:4-5#2/r1.claim: He says yāʾ is omitted in connected speech in favor of the kasra and omitted at pause with the kasra.

QURTUBI-FULL:89:4-5#2/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:89:4-5#2/r2.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:89:4-5#2/r2.claim: The oath nouns are genitive and its answer is omitted; the threat of punishment in 89:13 supplies it.

QURTUBI-FULL:89:4-5#2/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:89:4-5#2/r3.speaker: ابن الأنباري
QURTUBI-FULL:89:4-5#2/r3.claim: He says the omitted oath answer is 'Your Lord is ever watchful' in 89:14.

QURTUBI-FULL:89:4-5/r1.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:89:4-5/r1.speaker: القتبي والأخفش
QURTUBI-FULL:89:4-5/r1.claim: They explain yusrī as the night in which an event takes place, like a sleeping night or fasting day; the phrase links to 34:33.

QURTUBI-FULL:89:4-5/r10.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:89:4-5/r10.speaker: المؤرج عن الأخفش
QURTUBI-FULL:89:4-5/r10.claim: Al-Akhfash says the night does not itself travel but is traveled in; shifting a word from its literal direction weakens its inflection.

QURTUBI-FULL:89:4-5/r11.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:89:4-5/r11.speaker: الخليل
QURTUBI-FULL:89:4-5/r11.claim: He says the yāʾ drops to match the verse endings; al-Farra adds that Arabs may drop it while retaining the preceding kasra, supported by poetry.

QURTUBI-FULL:89:4-5/r12.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:89:4-5/r12.speaker: أهل الشام والكوفة وأبو عبيد
QURTUBI-FULL:89:4-5/r12.claim: The deletion reading is used in Syria and Kufa and preferred by Abu Ubayd because the written codex omits yāʾ.

QURTUBI-FULL:89:4-5/r13.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:89:4-5/r13.speaker: الكسائي
QURTUBI-FULL:89:4-5/r13.claim: Al-Kisa'i first retained yāʾ in connected reading and dropped it at pause, then adopted deletion in both positions to follow the consonantal text.

QURTUBI-FULL:89:4-5/r2.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:89:4-5/r2.speaker: أكثر المفسرين
QURTUBI-FULL:89:4-5/r2.claim: Most commentators say yusrī means the night went away.

QURTUBI-FULL:89:4-5/r3.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:89:4-5/r3.speaker: قتادة وأبو العالية
QURTUBI-FULL:89:4-5/r3.claim: They say the night came and approached.

QURTUBI-FULL:89:4-5/r4.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:89:4-5/r4.speaker: إبراهيم
QURTUBI-FULL:89:4-5/r4.claim: He interprets the night as having reached its midpoint or become even.

QURTUBI-FULL:89:4-5/r5.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:89:4-5/r5.speaker: عكرمة والكلبي ومجاهد ومحمد بن كعب
QURTUBI-FULL:89:4-5/r5.claim: They identify the night as the special night at Muzdalifa, when people gather in worship.

QURTUBI-FULL:89:4-5/r6.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:89:4-5/r6.speaker: بعض المفسرين
QURTUBI-FULL:89:4-5/r6.claim: Another view is the Night of Decree, when mercy flows and reward is increased.

QURTUBI-FULL:89:4-5/r7.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:89:4-5/r7.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:89:4-5/r7.claim: He prefers the general meaning of the whole night.

QURTUBI-FULL:89:4-5/r8.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:89:4-5/r8.speaker: ابن كثير وابن محيصن ويعقوب
QURTUBI-FULL:89:4-5/r8.claim: They retain the yāʾ of yusrī both in connected reading and pause, following the original form.

QURTUBI-FULL:89:4-5/r9.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:89:4-5/r9.speaker: نافع وأبو عمرو
QURTUBI-FULL:89:4-5/r9.claim: They retain the yāʾ when joining and drop it when pausing; the transmitted Kisa'i reading is also mentioned.

BAYDAWI-FULL:89:4-6/r1.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:89:4-6/r1.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:89:4-6/r1.claim: The night passes, as in 74:33; its restriction highlights the power and blessing in alternation, or derives from language for walking at night.

BAYDAWI-FULL:89:4-6/r2.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:89:4-6/r2.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:89:4-6/r2.claim: The final ياء may be omitted for ease; Nafiʿ and Abū ʿAmr omit it only at pauses for rhyme, while Ibn Kathīr and Yaʿqūb never omit it; another reading uses tanwin for a lengthening marker.

NASAFI-FULL:v4p336#4/r1.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v4p336#4/r1.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v4p336#4/r1.claim: “The night” may mean the Night of Decree; yasri means it passes, though its final yāʾ is dropped in connected recitation and at pause.

NASAFI-FULL:v4p336#4/r2.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v4p336#4/r2.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v4p336#4/r2.claim: When asked why the yāʾ is absent, al-Akhfash first said the questioner must serve him a year, then explained that night does not travel but one travels within it; transferred usage permits “a sleeping night.”

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p468/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p468/r5.speaker: أبو الدينار الأعرابي
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p468/r5.claim: Abu al-Dinar al-Aʿrabi adds tanwin to al-fajr, al-watr, and yasr; Ibn Khalawayh compares the usage with Arabs' pausal tanwin at rhyme endings, even on verbs or definite forms.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p469/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p469/r4.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p469/r4.claim: Most delete the yāʾ in yasr both connected and paused; Ibn Kathir retains it in both, while Nafiʿ and Ibn ʿAmr retain it only in connection.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p470#2/r1.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p470#2/r1.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p470#2/r1.claim: The night is sworn by as a kind, and yasr means it passes and disappears, as in the wording “when it departs.”

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p470#2/r2.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p470#2/r2.speaker: الأخفش وابن قتيبة
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p470#2/r2.claim: Al-Akhfash and Ibn Qutayba instead take yasr as night moving within itself, like the expression “your night is asleep.”

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p470#2/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p470#2/r3.speaker: مجاهد وعكرمة والكلبي
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p470#2/r3.claim: Mujahid, ʿIkrima, and al-Kalbi identify the night as the night at Jamʿ, when people travel through it.

SAMIN-DURR:89:4#2/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:89:4#2/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:89:4#2/r1.claim: ‘Idha yasri’ is governed by an omitted verb of swearing: ‘I swear by it at the time it travels by night’.

SAMIN-DURR:89:4#2/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:89:4#2/r2.speaker: نافع، أبو عمرو
SAMIN-DURR:89:4#2/r2.claim: Nafi‘ and Abu ‘Amr omit the yā’ of ‘yasri’ at pause but retain it in connected recitation.

SAMIN-DURR:89:4#2/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:89:4#2/r3.speaker: ابن كثير
SAMIN-DURR:89:4#2/r3.claim: Ibn Kathir retains the yā’ in both pausal and connected forms; the other readers omit it in both.

SAMIN-DURR:89:4#2/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:89:4#2/r4.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:89:4#2/r4.claim: Retention follows the original imperfect ending; omission follows the written muṣḥaf and verse cadence, like rhyme, while readers who distinguish pause treat it as a resting point.

SAMIN-DURR:89:4#2/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:89:4#2/r5.speaker: الأخفش
SAMIN-DURR:89:4#2/r5.claim: Al-Akhfash says night is figuratively described as traveling, though what is meant is that something travels through it.

SAMIN-DURR:89:4#2/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:89:4#2/r6.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:89:4#2/r6.claim: Another interpretation is that the night wanes, as in ‘idha adbara’ and ‘idha ‘as‘asa’.

SAMIN-DURR:89:4/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:89:4/r3.speaker: أبو الدينار الأعرابي
SAMIN-DURR:89:4/r3.claim: Most readers do not nunate ‘al-fajr’, ‘al-watr’, and ‘yasr’; Abu al-Dinar al-A‘rabi nunates all three, treating verse endings like poetic rhymes.

SAMIN-DURR:89:4/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:89:4/r4.speaker: ابن خالويه
SAMIN-DURR:89:4/r4.claim: Ibn Khalawayh calls the poetic nunation ‘tanwin al-tarannum’, including nunation at verse endings even for verbs and definite nouns; his quoted couplet illustrates it.

SAMIN-DURR:89:4/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:89:4/r5.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:89:4/r5.claim: Some grammarians object to the label ‘tanwin al-tarannum’ and prefer ‘tanwin tark al-tarannum’; another type, ‘tanwin al-ghali’, appears on a closed rhyme and is disputed, with different rules from ordinary nunation.

SAMIN-DURR:89:4/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:89:4/r6.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:89:4/r6.claim: The reader has treated the Qur’anic endings like rhyme endings; the author cites similar forms in al-Ahzab and al-Ra‘d as parallels.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p393#2/r1.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p393#2/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p393#2/r1.claim: Ibn Abbas says the night is departing; Ibn al-Zubayr describes it as one portion of night following another until it is gone.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p393#2/r2.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p393#2/r2.speaker: مجاهد
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p393#2/r2.claim: Mujahid, Abu al-Aliyah, Qatadah, and others understand the night as moving or traveling.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p393#2/r3.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p393#2/r3.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p393#2/r3.claim: Ibn Kathir allows both departure and movement, but says movement better balances dawn: night arrives as day departs, like the paired oath in Surat al-Takwir.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p393#2/r4.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p393#2/r4.speaker: الضحاك
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p393#2/r4.claim: Al-Dahhak glosses the night as running along.

IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p393#2/r5.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p393#2/r5.speaker: عكرمة
IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p393#2/r5.claim: Ikrimah interprets the night as the night of Muzdalifah; Muhammad ibn Ka'b adds that it is only clear at Jam, another name for Muzdalifah.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p413#2/r6.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p413#2/r6.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p413#2/r6.claim: The night of departure passes as worldly night passes and dawn replaces its darkness; pilgrims return to their homes after laying down their burdens.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p413#2/r7.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p413#2/r7.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p413#2/r7.claim: Ibn Kathir and Yaʿqub retain the final yāʾ in yasri, while the other readers omit it.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p413#2/r8.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p413#2/r8.speaker: الأخفش
BIQAI-FULL:v8p413#2/r8.claim: Asked why the final yāʾ was omitted, al-Akhfash answered that night is traveled in rather than itself traveling, so the altered sense requires an altered form; the author says this entails rejecting transmitted affirmation readings.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p414/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p414/r1.speaker: الأخفش
BIQAI-FULL:v8p414/r1.claim: Al-Akhfash analogizes the omitted yāʾ in yasri to baghiy, ‘unchaste,’ rather than baghiya, ‘unchaste woman’; the author says this linguistic rationale rejects transmitted readings that affirm the yāʾ.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p414/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p414/r2.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p414/r2.claim: Omission may signal pilgrims who remain at the sacred sites, savoring the night, while affirmation may signal those whose full night has passed as they return home at dawn.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p414/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p414/r3.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p414/r3.claim: Alternatively, omission points to a short night and affirmation to a long one, with worshippers standing through the long night before the King.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p414/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p414/r4.speaker: تقي الدين بن دقيق العيد
BIQAI-FULL:v8p414/r4.claim: Ibn Daqiq al-ʿId’s verse evokes nights of traveling through the night without sleep or rest, supporting the long-night interpretation.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p414/r5.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p414/r5.speaker: أبو طالب
BIQAI-FULL:v8p414/r5.claim: Abu Talib’s poem invokes the night at Muzdalifah and the stations of Mina as sacred gathering places.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p414/r6.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p414/r6.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p414/r6.claim: Differences in night length and in the travelers’ situations show that one sovereign Creator freely controls all these signs and can destroy tyrants.

DURR-FULL:v8p503/r10.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p503/r10.speaker: مجاهد
DURR-FULL:v8p503/r10.claim: He also explained the night as it travels on.

DURR-FULL:v8p503/r11.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p503/r11.speaker: عكرمة
DURR-FULL:v8p503/r11.claim: He identified it as the night at Muzdalifah (Jamʿ).

DURR-FULL:v8p503/r12.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p503/r12.speaker: محمد بن كعب القرظي
DURR-FULL:v8p503/r12.claim: He understood it as the departure from Muzdalifah, quoting the instruction to travel by night and not spend the night anywhere but Jamʿ.

DURR-FULL:v8p503/r13.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p503/r13.speaker: ابن مسعود
DURR-FULL:v8p503/r13.claim: His recitation ran from the dawn oath through the night oath; he said these oaths affirm that the Lord is ever watchful.

DURR-FULL:v8p503/r8.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p503/r8.speaker: ابن عباس
DURR-FULL:v8p503/r8.claim: He explained the night as it departs.

DURR-FULL:v8p503/r9.author: al-Suyūṭī
DURR-FULL:v8p503/r9.speaker: عبد الله بن الزبير
DURR-FULL:v8p503/r9.claim: He explained the night as it travels on.

BURSEVI:v10p326#2/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p326#2/r1.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v10p326#2/r1.claim: The phrase about night passing can mean travelers move through it; night protects them from heat and often from highwaymen, and the Prophet recommended night travel because the earth is folded then.

BURSEVI:v10p326#2/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p326#2/r2.speaker: الأخفش
BURSEVI:v10p326#2/r2.claim: When asked about the missing yā in “yasr,” al-Akhfash first had no answer, then explained that night is traveled through rather than traveling, so the form was altered to mark the shift in meaning.

BURSEVI:v10p326#2/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p326#2/r4.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v10p326#2/r4.claim: Inwardly, the passing night can symbolize the self’s darkness disappearing as spirit is stripped bare, the absolute night of identity flowing into the day of determinate realities, or the Prophet’s supreme Night Journey.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p121#2/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p121#2/r1.speaker: أبو حيان
ALUSI-FULL:v30p121#2/r1.claim: Abu Hayyan says tanwīn at verse endings treats them as unrestrained poetic rhymes; Arabs either retain the final vowel without tarannum or pause on the word as in prose.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p121#2/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p121#2/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p121#2/r2.claim: This Bedouin treated the verse endings like pauses and unrestrained rhyme endings; the tanwīn is called tanwīn al-tarannum and is not exclusive to nouns.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p121#2/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p121#2/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p121#2/r3.claim: Alusi suspects that the tanwīn was written with a nūn, unlike the categories of tanwīn restricted to nouns.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p121/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p121/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p121/r1.claim: Yasri means the night passes, as in 74:33 and 81:17; the expression is figurative, and the oath concerns the generic night.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p121/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p121/r2.speaker: التفتازاني
ALUSI-FULL:v30p121/r2.claim: Al-Taftazani says idha is a substitute for “night”; others attach it to an omitted word such as “majesty,” since the oath is not meant to be temporally restricted.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p121/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p121/r3.speaker: الأخفش وابن قتيبة
ALUSI-FULL:v30p121/r3.claim: Al-Akhfash and Ibn Qutayba allow yasri to mean that people travel through the night, with the action attributed figuratively to its time.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p121/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p121/r4.speaker: مجاهد وعكرمة والكلبي
ALUSI-FULL:v30p121/r4.claim: Mujahid, Ikrima, and al-Kalbi identify the night as the night of sacrifice, when pilgrims travel to Muzdalifa after leaving Arafat; Alusi says this is not well-founded.

ALUSI-FULL:v30p121/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v30p121/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v30p121/r5.claim: Interpreting the oath as restricted to pilgrims' travel is weak; if night travel is intended, its protection from the Sun's heat and highway robbers is the blessing in view.

ELMALILI:89:4-7/r1.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:89:4-7/r1.speaker: author
ELMALILI:89:4-7/r1.claim: The oath is by night as it passes, as in the similar wording of 74:33.

ELMALILI:89:4-7/r2.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:89:4-7/r2.speaker: author
ELMALILI:89:4-7/r2.claim: The original form is yesrī; the final yāʾ is omitted for rhyme, so the kasra on rāʾ does not mark jussive mood; some canonical readings retain the yāʾ.

ELMALILI:89:4-7/r3.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:89:4-7/r3.speaker: author
ELMALILI:89:4-7/r3.claim: Nafi, Abu Amr, and Abu Jafar retain yāʾ in connected recitation; Ibn Kathir and Yaqub retain it both in pause and connection.

ELMALILI:89:4-7/r4.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:89:4-7/r4.speaker: author
ELMALILI:89:4-7/r4.claim: The wording intensifies the idea of night traveling within the night; beyond the usual bare sense of passing, it can suggest darkness about to end and grief about to pass at the blessed pre-dawn hour.

ELMALILI:89:4-7/r5.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:89:4-7/r5.speaker: author
ELMALILI:89:4-7/r5.claim: Generic night and dawn have the widest scope, though the night before the feast dawn is more cohesive and splendid; some identify it as the night of gathering at Muzdalifa.

QUTB-ZILAL:89:4/r1.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:89:4/r1.speaker: author
QUTB-ZILAL:89:4/r1.claim: Night is personified as a living traveler moving through the cosmos, perhaps a wakeful wanderer or one choosing the night journey; this delicately matches dawn and the preceding oaths.

QUTB-ZILAL:89:4/r2.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:89:4/r2.speaker: author
QUTB-ZILAL:89:4/r2.claim: The phrasing and scene create a gentle, fragrant, intimate beauty that joins the heart, spirit, and conscience through subtle suggestion.

IBNASHUR:89:4/r1.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:89:4/r1.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:89:4/r1.claim: Night is coordinated with the ten nights as a general after a specific, or with dawn because the two oppose each other; it is an oath because night displays God's power and wisdom.

IBNASHUR:89:4/r2.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:89:4/r2.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:89:4/r2.claim: Yasri means to move through darkness: much of the night has elapsed, figuratively likened to a traveler's nocturnal journey.

IBNASHUR:89:4/r3.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:89:4/r3.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:89:4/r3.claim: The expression is compared with night retreating or becoming still and dark in other passages.

IBNASHUR:89:4/r4.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:89:4/r4.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:89:4/r4.claim: The time clause marks the settled darkness, when people have slept enough to perform night vigil.

IBNASHUR:89:4/r5.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:89:4/r5.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:89:4/r5.claim: Nafi, Abu Amr, Abu Ja'far, and Yaqub read the final ya in connected recitation but omit it at a pause to preserve the rhyme endings.

IBNASHUR:89:4/r6.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:89:4/r6.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:89:4/r6.claim: Quranic verse endings function like prose assonance and receive treatment like poetic rhyme; Abu Ali says deletion at a pause is no worse than retention, while outside a rhyme retention is better.

IBNASHUR:89:4/r7.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:89:4/r7.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:89:4/r7.claim: Ibn Kathir and Yaqub are also said to retain the ya both in connection and at a pause, following the underlying form.

IBNASHUR:89:4/r8.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:89:4/r8.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:89:4/r8.claim: The other readers omit the ya in both positions, matching the Quranic codex spelling; readers who retain it follow transmitted recitation and treat the spelling as a pause form or as canonical practice.

IBNASHUR:89:4/r9.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:89:4/r9.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:89:4/r9.claim: The codex spelling does not weaken Nafi, Abu Amr, and Abu Ja'far's connected-reading tradition because Quranic spelling often reflects pausal pronunciation.

TABATABAI:89:5-8/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:89:5-8/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:89:5-8/r1.claim: Yasri means passes on, as in 74:33; the definite article is generic, so the oath concerns the end of night generally.

TABATABAI:89:5-8/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:89:5-8/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:89:5-8/r2.claim: A reported alternative identifies the night as the Night of Sacrifice, when pilgrims travel from Arafat to Muzdalifa and then Mina; the author finds this implausible, especially if the ten nights are the first ten nights.

ASAD-NOTES:89:1#n3/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:89:1#n3/r1.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:89:1#n3/r1.claim: The night running its course alludes to spiritual darkness disappearing when a person becomes conscious of God.

BINTSHATI:v2p132/r3.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v2p132/r3.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v2p132/r3.claim: The author rejects forced interpretations that turn even, odd, dawn, and night into honorific objects; their contrast directs attention to sensory realities.

BINTSHATI:v2p132/r4.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v2p132/r4.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v2p132/r4.claim: The Quranic oath's rhetorical function is to direct attention to perceptible dawn breaking through night, preparing readers for unseen meanings of guidance and error.

BINTSHATI:v2p133/r1.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v2p133/r1.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v2p133/r1.claim: Assigning the journey to night is a grammatical metaphor based on time, but the literary expression goes beyond this conventional label.

BINTSHATI:v2p133/r2.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v2p133/r2.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v2p133/r2.claim: Attributing travel to night is a time-based metaphor, but personifies night as an active living traveler and fuses the event with its time.

BINTSHATI:v2p133/r3.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v2p133/r3.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v2p133/r3.claim: The root appears eight Quranic times: seven are night-travel verbs and one is the brook called sariyy in Mary's story.

BINTSHATI:v2p133/r4.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v2p133/r4.speaker: مقاتل
BINTSHATI:v2p133/r4.claim: Al-Tabari transmits from Muqatil that the verse means the night at Muzdalifah and that the traveler is the pilgrim; the author says the general wording resists this restriction.

BINTSHATI:v2p133/r5.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v2p133/r5.speaker: أبو حيان
BINTSHATI:v2p133/r5.claim: Abu Hayyan and al-Naysaburi read the phrase as night passing, while Ibn al-Qayyim allows its arrival or departure.

BINTSHATI:v2p133/r6.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v2p133/r6.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v2p133/r6.claim: The author finds a simple departure or arrival too narrow because sara spans the whole night from beginning to end.

BINTSHATI:v2p133/r7.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v2p133/r7.speaker: محمد عبده
BINTSHATI:v2p133/r7.claim: Muhammad Abdu takes night to mean darkness, but the author rejects ignoring the qualifiers attached to night in Quranic oaths.

BINTSHATI:v2p134/r1.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v2p134/r1.speaker: محمد عبده
BINTSHATI:v2p134/r1.claim: Muhammad Abdu argues that moonlit, dark nights stir emotion, travel, hopes, and fears, making them fitting objects of solemn oath; dawn relieves night and prompts work.

BINTSHATI:v2p134/r2.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v2p134/r2.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v2p134/r2.claim: The author calls Abdu's case contrived: mid-month nights are more attractive for moonlit talk, and darkness cannot explain an oath that celebrates dawn's relief.

BINTSHATI:v2p134/r3.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v2p134/r3.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v2p134/r3.claim: The oath's waw redirects attention from honorification to an undeniable sensory scene that prepares persuasion about disputed unseen matters.

BINTSHATI:v2p135/r1.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v2p135/r1.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v2p135/r1.claim: The author rejects readings that inflate every oath object into a symbol of honor and confuse exaltation with divine wisdom in creation.

BINTSHATI:v2p135/r2.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v2p135/r2.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v2p135/r2.claim: The succession of dawn, crescent, and night makes sensory light and darkness an image of truth emerging after prolonged moral darkness and tyranny.

BINTSHATI:v2p135/r3.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v2p135/r3.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v2p135/r3.claim: The natural contrasts prepare for testing through wealth or deprivation and the opposed outcomes of tyrants and the tranquil soul.

BINTSHATI:v2p135/r4.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v2p135/r4.speaker: الطبري
BINTSHATI:v2p135/r4.claim: Al-Tabari says the verses should not be burdened with claims unsupported by transmitted reports or reason; al-Razi and al-Zamakhshari also criticize the commentators' sprawling speculation.

BINTSHATI:v2p136/r1.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v2p136/r1.speaker: الزمخشري
BINTSHATI:v2p136/r1.claim: The author says the surrounding passage is better read as a call to admonition and reflection.

BINTSHATI:v2p136/r2.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v2p136/r2.speaker: الفخر الرازي
BINTSHATI:v2p136/r2.claim: Al-Razi identifies 'your Lord is surely watching' as the oath's answer and treats the intervening passage as parenthetical.

BINTSHATI:v2p136/r3.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v2p136/r3.speaker: ابن القيم
BINTSHATI:v2p136/r3.claim: Ibn al-Qayyim takes the answer as implicit in the oath's inclusion of what was brought to Abraham and Muhammad.

BINTSHATI:v2p136/r4.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v2p136/r4.speaker: أوب حيان
BINTSHATI:v2p136/r4.claim: Abu Hayyan and Muhammad Abdu say the omitted answer is the end of al-Ghashiya, because that surah precedes al-Fajr in the printed Quran.

BINTSHATI:v2p136/r5.author: ʿĀʾisha ʿAbd al-Raḥmān (Bint al-Shāṭiʾ)
BINTSHATI:v2p136/r5.speaker: author
BINTSHATI:v2p136/r5.claim: The author rejects an answer supplied by al-Ghashiya: it was revealed 58 surahs after al-Fajr, so adjacency in the printed order cannot leave this oath suspended until then.

CORPUSCORANICUM:89:1-4:anmerkung/r1.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:89:1-4:anmerkung/r1.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:89:1-4:anmerkung/r1.claim: Qur'anic oath formulas probably draw on a characteristic expression of pre-Islamic soothsayers, though this connection remains insufficiently studied.

CORPUSCORANICUM:89:1-4:anmerkung/r2.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:89:1-4:anmerkung/r2.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:89:1-4:anmerkung/r2.claim: For the oath type in this passage, the commentary directs readers to its discussion of 93:1–2.

CORPUSCORANICUM:89:1-5:kommentar/r1.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:89:1-5:kommentar/r1.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:89:1-5:kommentar/r1.claim: The opening oath resembles those in earlier suras 93, 95, 100, and 103 and roughly contemporary suras 91 and 92.

CORPUSCORANICUM:89:1-5:kommentar/r2.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:89:1-5:kommentar/r2.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:89:1-5:kommentar/r2.claim: The oath's cosmic oppositions, day/night and odd/even, resemble 91 and 92, where such duality anticipates moral and afterlife oppositions.

CORPUSCORANICUM:89:1-5:kommentar/r6.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:89:1-5:kommentar/r6.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:89:1-5:kommentar/r6.claim: The oath also tracks time: ten nights suggest a likely cultic period, while single/even units and the night passage evoke measurable spans and temporal flow.

CORPUSCORANICUM:89:1-5:kommentar/r7.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:89:1-5:kommentar/r7.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:89:1-5:kommentar/r7.claim: The temporal emphasis may relate to this being among the earliest texts to give historical examples of God's punishment.

CORPUSCORANICUM:89:4:anmerkung/r1.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:89:4:anmerkung/r1.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:89:4:anmerkung/r1.claim: This oath follows a recurring formula, wa-l-laili ʾiḏā plus a verb, also used in several early suras.

CORPUSCORANICUM:89:4:anmerkung/r2.author: Nicolai Sinai (Frühmekkanische Suren), with Nora K. Schmid, using preparatory work by Angelika Neuwirth; later parts Dirk Hartwig, Angelika Neuwirth et al. (author line per sura in segments)
CORPUSCORANICUM:89:4:anmerkung/r2.speaker: author
CORPUSCORANICUM:89:4:anmerkung/r2.claim: The shortened yasr, suppressing the short vowel found in poetry, probably stands for yasrī to preserve the rhyme.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p296/r1.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p296/r1.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p296/r1.claim: The preceding surah's signs establish God's power, wisdom, and providence, which entail a Day of accountability and reward; otherwise His mercy and wisdom would be contradicted.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p296/r2.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p296/r2.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p296/r2.claim: The Prophet's role is to warn through the signs in heaven and earth, even when people cannot see them; he cannot guide the blind.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p299/r1.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p299/r1.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p299/r1.claim: The oaths establish that God alone governs the world, brings things forth and removes them, grants respite, and acts within no rival's authority.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p299/r3.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p299/r3.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p299/r3.claim: The dawn oath resembles oaths in al-Muddaththir: night recedes and morning appears as evidence that the Day of Judgment is a great event.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p300/r3.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p300/r3.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p300/r3.claim: Oaths should be read as evidence for the surah's claim, not assumed to concern sacred objects; identify the claim and compare parallel Qur'anic passages.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p302/r4.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p302/r4.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p302/r4.claim: The night oath focuses on the moment it begins to depart and dawn's first signs appear.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p303/r1.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p303/r1.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p303/r1.claim: Night's hold seems total, yet dawn overwhelms it, showing that all worldly elements submit to God.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p303/r2.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p303/r2.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p303/r2.claim: The night giving way to day symbolizes Judgment for people who consider it remote.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p303/r3.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p303/r3.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p303/r3.claim: Those who think Judgment is far away should know that by God's measure it is near to this world; the Prophet likens their nearness to two adjacent fingers.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p303/r4.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p303/r4.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p303/r4.claim: The phrase idha yasri also teaches that trials are temporary and train the soul; people should face them with gratitude and perseverance, trusting hidden good.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p303/r5.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p303/r5.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p303/r5.claim: The first and last oaths are primary and contrast dawn with departing night; the middle oaths are secondary signs between them supporting the opening claim.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p304/r1.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p304/r1.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p304/r1.claim: Contrasting forces of nature coexist in harmony; only one wise, powerful sovereign can reconcile them, since competing deities would destroy the world.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p304/r2.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p304/r2.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p304/r2.claim: Pairs reach completion with their counterparts; likewise this world is incomplete without an afterlife, where God will judge the conflict of good and evil and reward or punish people.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p305/r1.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p305/r1.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p305/r1.claim: Without a Day of Judgment, good and evil would be treated alike and creation would be purposeless; 68:35–36 makes the same objection to denying accountability.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p305/r2.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p305/r2.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p305/r2.claim: Daylight and night sustain material life, while ease and hardship train the moral and spiritual self in gratitude and patience, preparing people for the state described in 89:28.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p305/r3.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p305/r3.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p305/r3.claim: The alternation of night and day shows that every created thing is governed by God, so even powerful people cannot escape His control.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p305/r4.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p305/r4.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p305/r4.claim: The oath's signs of release and restraint emphasize God's control, as illustrated by the possibility of perpetual night or day in 28:71–72.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:89:1/r10.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:89:1/r10.speaker: Müfessirler
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:89:1/r10.claim: The unstated oath's answer is taken either to affirm resurrection, Judgment, punishment, and reward, or to be verse 14: God watches all, knows deeds, and recompenses them.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:89:1/r7.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:89:1/r7.speaker: Müfessirler
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:89:1/r7.claim: Some identify the passing night as the night at Muzdalifah or the festival night.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:89:1/r8.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:89:1/r8.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:89:1/r8.claim: The unrestricted wording and the Qur'an's other general cosmic oaths make all nights the preferable meaning.

QIRAAT-ER:89:4:4#1/r1.author: QIRAAT-ER
QIRAAT-ER:89:4:4#1/r1.speaker: author
QIRAAT-ER:89:4:4#1/r1.claim: Restoring final weak yāʾ makes the imperfect phonetically full while preserving root and meaning.

QIRAAT-ER:89:4:4#2/r1.author: QIRAAT-ER
QIRAAT-ER:89:4:4#2/r1.speaker: author
QIRAAT-ER:89:4:4#2/r1.claim: The pausal clipped yasr contrasts with full yasrī, focusing recitational pressure on the final weak letter.

SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p410/r1.author: فاضل صالح السامرائي
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p410/r1.speaker: author
SAMARRAI-LAMASAT-HALAQAT:p410/r1.claim: Sajā brings together stillness and darkness, matching revelation's suspension and loss of light; yaghshā and yasri imply movement and therefore fit less well.

STUDYQURAN:89:4/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:89:4/r1.speaker: most commentators
STUDYQURAN:89:4/r1.claim: Most commentators understand the verse as night in general, indicating God's wisdom in measuring night and day.

STUDYQURAN:89:4/r2.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:89:4/r2.speaker: some
STUDYQURAN:89:4/r2.claim: Some take it as the Hajj night when pilgrims gather at Muzdalifah before moving to Minā.

STUDYQURAN:89:4/r3.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:89:4/r3.speaker: others
STUDYQURAN:89:4/r3.claim: Others understand it as the Night of Power.
